title: Durvalumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin
context_label: First-line dMMR/MSI-H advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer
therapy_label: Immunotherapy and chemotherapy, followed by immunotherapy alone
schedule_label: Combination every 21 days → durvalumab alone every 28 days
schedule_summary: Day 1 every 21 days: all three medicines for 4–6 cycles. If continuing, durvalumab alone starts 3 weeks after the last combination infusion, then repeats every 28 days while helping and tolerated.
purpose: The aim is to control the cancer, ease or prevent symptoms and delay worsening. Your team can explain the benefit they expect for you and your other options.
indication_text: First treatment for womb (endometrial) cancer that is advanced or has returned, when curative surgery or radiotherapy is unsuitable and a tumour test shows deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H). These changes can make the tumour more visible to immune cells.
administration_text: All medicines are given into a vein. On combination days durvalumab is given first over about 1 hour, then paclitaxel over about 3 hours and carboplatin over about 30 minutes. Allow extra time for review, premedicines, blood results and preparation. Durvalumab alone takes about an hour.
monitoring_summary: Before treatment the team checks your tumour result, full blood count, kidney and liver function, thyroid hormones and random blood sugar. Kidney filtration helps set the carboplatin dose. The team asks about tingling or hearing problems and arranges extra tests when indicated.
review_status: Independent clinical, pharmacy and patient review pending
phases_note: Your team records the actual last combination date. A delay changes your calendar.

agents.name: Durvalumab
agents.explanation: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a signal that can slow an immune attack. This can help immune cells recognise cancer, but sometimes causes inflammation in healthy organs.
agents.mechanism: Durvalumab blocks PD-L1, a signal that can slow an immune attack. This can help immune cells recognise cancer, but sometimes causes inflammation in healthy organs.
visual: Cancer can use PD-L1 as a brake
risks: Immune inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin and hormone glands.
Rare heart, muscle or nerve inflammation can be serious.
agents.watch: New cough, breathlessness, diarrhoea or severe weakness needs urgent advice.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel prevents cells from completing division. It can also injure growing hair and blood cells and affect nerves in hands and feet.
agents.mechanism: Paclitaxel prevents cells from completing division. It can also injure growing hair and blood cells and affect nerves in hands and feet.
risks: Hair loss, aching muscles or joints, tingling and numbness.
Low blood counts and allergic reactions during infusion.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, wheezing or dizziness during infusion; mention new numbness before the next dose.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.alias: Combination visits only; dose uses kidney function.
agents.explanation: Carboplatin links strands of DNA inside cells, making it difficult for dividing cancer cells to copy their DNA. Blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.mechanism: Carboplatin links strands of DNA inside cells, making it difficult for dividing cancer cells to copy their DNA. Blood-forming cells can also be affected.
risks: Low blood counts, infection or bleeding.
agents.watch: Call oncology urgently for fever, chills, unexplained bruising or bleeding.

common_effects.title: Tiredness
common_effects.text: Plan rest around visits and report fatigue that is new, severe or associated with dizziness.

common_effects.title: Nausea and appetite changes
common_effects.text: During combination therapy take the anti-sickness medicines on your plan and report difficulty drinking.

common_effects.title: Hair loss, aches and tingling
common_effects.text: Paclitaxel can cause hair loss, muscle aches and numb or painful fingers or toes. Report nerve symptoms early.

serious_effects.title: Pneumonitis · lung inflammation
serious_effects.text: New cough or breathlessness needs an immediate oncology call. Severe breathing difficulty needs 112 or 999.

serious_effects.title: Infection or low blood counts
serious_effects.text: Fever, chills or sudden illness can be serious even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately.

serious_effects.title: Colitis · bowel inflammation
serious_effects.text: New or worsening diarrhoea, belly pain or blood in stools needs urgent oncology advice.

serious_effects.title: Hormone problems
serious_effects.text: Severe weakness, dizziness, vomiting or extreme thirst can signal changes in hormone or blood-sugar levels. Call oncology immediately.

serious_effects.title: Infusion allergy
serious_effects.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, wheezy, dizzy or unwell during a drip.

anatomy: Call urgently for new cough or breathlessness.
Call urgently about severe headache, dizziness, thirst or unusual weakness.
Severe chest pain or collapse needs 112 or 999.
Call urgently for new diarrhoea, pain or blood in stools.
Yellow eyes or dark urine need urgent advice. Blood tests may find inflammation early.
Hair loss can occur. A blistering or peeling rash needs urgent advice.
Report new tingling, numbness or trouble walking or fastening buttons before the next infusion.
Fever, shaking chills, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs an immediate oncology call.
anatomy_note: Symptoms can overlap between medicines. Contact your team without trying to identify which drug caused them.

chronology_notes.title: Moving between phases
chronology_notes.text: The first single-drug infusion is planned 3 weeks after your last combination dose. Later maintenance doses are 4 weeks apart.

chronology_notes.title: If treatment is delayed
chronology_notes.text: A clinician changes your dates or dose. Never use a calendar or stamp to decide whether treatment can proceed.

sections.title: On a combination day
sections.text: All medicines are given into a vein. On combination days durvalumab is given first over about 1 hour, then paclitaxel over about 3 hours and carboplatin over about 30 minutes. Allow extra time for review, premedicines, blood results and preparation. Durvalumab alone takes about an hour.

sections.title: Before your visit
sections.text: Bring your medicines list, alert card and 24-hour oncology contact. Tell the team about prior allergic reactions, hearing issues, diabetes, autoimmune disease, steroids and nerve symptoms.

sections.title: Leaving the unit
sections.text: Write down the date of the next blood test, the next infusion and the 24-hour phone number. Confirm whether the next visit is for three drugs or one.

evidence.title: What the trial found
evidence.intro: DUO-E compared chemotherapy plus durvalumab followed by durvalumab maintenance against chemotherapy alone with placebo.
evidence.population: People with newly diagnosed advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. The Irish regimen is limited to the dMMR/MSI-H group.
evidence.interpretation: The dMMR subgroup receiving durvalumab had a lower rate of progression or death over follow-up (hazard ratio 0.42, 95% confidence interval 0.22–0.80). This compares groups over time and does not predict how long treatment will help one person.
evidence.limitations: This was a prespecified exploratory subgroup. A separate study arm also used olaparib; olaparib is not part of this NCCP regimen.

teachback: Which medicines do you get in each phase, when does maintenance begin, and what would you do if you felt feverish or developed a new cough at home?
consent_support: Discuss your treatment aim, alternatives including supportive care, the expected benefit and uncertainties, duration, infusion reactions, infection, low blood counts, hair loss, neuropathy and delayed immune inflammation. Ask about possible lifelong hormone treatment, fertility, contraception, breastfeeding, and what would prompt a pause or stop. You can ask more questions or reconsider your choice.

support.title: Preventing sickness
support.text: Combination treatment has high sickness risk, mainly from carboplatin. Take your prescribed prevention and rescue medicines as directed. Durvalumab alone has minimal sickness risk, so the plan may change.

support.title: Before paclitaxel
support.text: The team gives medicines to lower the chance of an infusion reaction, including a steroid and antihistamine according to its plan. Tell the nurse immediately about wheeze, flushing or faintness.

support.title: Nerve or muscle symptoms
support.text: Contact the team early about numb or painful hands or feet, difficulty with buttons or walking, or troublesome muscle or joint aches.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your immunotherapy alert card during and after treatment. Show it to any urgent-care clinician. Do not start, stop or change steroids yourself.

support.title: Fertility and pregnancy
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, contraception and fertility before treatment. Durvalumab requires effective contraception during treatment and for at least three months after the last dose; ask your team for the longest interval required by any medicine you receive. Do not breastfeed during treatment.

induction.title: Sickness plan for combination days
induction.text: Carboplatin has high risk of sickness. Your team prescribes medicines to prevent sickness and rescue medicines for home. Confirm names, times and what to do if you vomit or cannot drink.

induction.title: Before the taxane infusion
induction.text: The team gives medicines to reduce allergy risk before paclitaxel, according to local policy. Tell the nurse straight away about flushing, wheezing, pain or dizziness during an infusion.

induction.title: Home and urgent help
induction.text: Call oncology immediately for fever or sudden illness, new cough or breathing changes, persistent diarrhoea or unusual bleeding. Bring your immune alert card. Report tingling or trouble walking before the next cycle.

maintenance.title: Change of medicines
maintenance.text: Only durvalumab is planned. Its sickness risk is minimal, and the team reviews whether you still need rescue medicines. The taxane premedicines used during combination treatment are no longer part of a routine maintenance visit.

maintenance.title: Immune symptoms may be delayed
maintenance.text: Call urgently for new cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea or bloody stool, severe weakness, dizziness or a blistering rash during or after maintenance. Carry your immunotherapy alert card. Severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs 112 or 999.

maintenance.title: Current appointments
maintenance.text: The first maintenance infusion is planned three weeks after the last combination infusion; following visits are every four weeks. Confirm the next blood test, infusion and 24-hour contact before leaving.
